prize_parts.citation: For establishing that biomolecular condensates form by liquid-liquid phase separation, a physical-chemical principle for organizing the interior of cells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for biomolecular phase separation to Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. The thermodynamic description (concentration, multivalency and interaction strength setting when liquid droplets form, how they wet, age and sometimes harden) is a general principle, and it rests on two concrete, independently replicated anchors: the 2009 P-granule demonstration and the 2012 reconstitution of multivalent signalling proteins in vitro. The latter keeps the claim from being only a cell-imaging observation. After fifteen years the phenomenon is reproduced in hundreds of laboratories and has changed how amyloid, neurodegeneration and intracellular organisation are discussed. This is a new concept of molecular organisation, and physical chemistry is thinly represented among recent prizes.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which Linke, Aili and I all state, is that the physiological relevance of many specific condensates is still contested and parts of the literature rely on overexpression and imaging. Credit is the second problem: a three-name cap excludes Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar and sticker-spacer work gave the quantitative theory, and the Medicine committee could claim the 2009 discovery. B052 is the more mature and attribution-clean alternative, with four explicit supporters, and I cannot honestly claim B002 is closer to a majority today. I would accept B052 as a worthy outcome if the committee prefers certainty over conceptual novelty.

responses.point: Johan holds that Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is a game-changer with the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and that three decades of confirmation remove any maturity concern.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and the Buchwald-Hartwig pair, and I do not dispute the impact. I still read it as a new bond type within a catalytic paradigm that the 2010 prize already established, whereas condensates changed the framework for describing cell interiors. On the chair's Kosugi question, Johan and Peter Somfai both say they cannot settle priority from the files, while Zou says the tin-amide reaction was neither general nor ligand-controlled. If that is right, a citation worded around general, ligand-controlled coupling is defensible, but I would want the expert report to document it before the credit is called clean.

responses.point: Daniel proposes a two-part prize pairing B052 (Buchwald, Hartwig) with B004 (Liu alone), and treats B002 as possibly slightly early because physiological relevance is debated.
responses.response: I take the balance argument seriously; it is the only configuration that gives both a synthetic method and a biomolecular achievement. My difficulty is that Liu alone passes over Komor and Gaudelli, which Daniel himself acknowledges as the weakest point, and Target-AID remains an independent priority claim. A prize that must be allocated as two plus one to fit the cap does not seem more robust to me than a clean single part. On maturity I distinguish the physical phenomenon, which is replicated and textbook-level, from claims about particular condensates in vivo, which are the part still unsettled. A citation for the principle, not the physiological claims, answers his concern.

responses.point: Heiner supports B002 for Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen, adds multivalency principles to the citation, and acknowledges that B052 has the cleanest attribution and most opening support.
responses.response: We share the same configuration and we are colleagues at Lund, so agreement between us should carry little weight on its own. His multivalency wording is better physical chemistry than my original, but it narrows the citation toward Rosen's work and makes the omission of Pappu and Mittag more visible, so I would keep a citation about the principle of liquid-liquid phase separation. On the chair's Chemistry versus Medicine question, I think the in vitro multivalency and thermodynamics make this chemistry, and I would argue it on that basis rather than on the cell-biological one.

responses.point: Peter supports B052 on the test that the method is visible in countless later syntheses and in industry, and notes that a citation omitting Kosugi invites a priority argument.
responses.response: I agree with the test as applied to a method, and B052 passes it. I would apply a different test to a concept: whether it lets one predict behaviour that could not be predicted before. Condensates meet that by relating droplet formation to valency and concentration. His point that omitting Kosugi invites a priority argument is the practical weakness I would most like to see resolved, but I do not see it as fatal for B052, which is why I list B052 first among my alternatives.

responses.point: Andrei supports base editing as a clean chemical mechanism and ranks B002 only fourth, so his reservation about condensates was left open.
responses.response: Base editing is a good chemistry story and the directed evolution of the adenine deaminase is a fair point. It does not change my view, because Target-AID attribution is unresolved and the 2020 CRISPR prize makes the sequel question harder here than for B052 or B002. I also note the PROTAC credit problem he raised, which makes me think the three-name cap handles condensates better than degraders. I read his reservation about B002 as mostly about physiological relevance, which I share, rather than about the physical-chemical principle.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards condensates as chemistry rather than physiology or medicine
Whether the in vivo functional role of specific condensates is established well enough for a prize citation
Whether Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen fairly represent the discovery with Pappu and Mittag left out
Whether Kosugi's tin-amide work is documented as non-general, which determines whether B052 is clean
Whether B002 can reach five votes against four explicit supporters of B052
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1: I am at Lund with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my research on lipid self-assembly and amyloid is close to condensate biophysics, though I have no collaboration with the proposed laureates. No recusal is required; I flag the field closeness and shared institution for transparency, and agreement with Linke should not be counted as independent support.
